claim: m6A is the most widespread mRNA modification.
source: m6A is the most widespread mRNA modification and is primarily implicated in controlling mRNA stability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about m6A.

claim: m6A is primarily implicated in controlling mRNA stability.
source: m6A is the most widespread mRNA modification and is primarily implicated in controlling mRNA stability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal modification in mammalian mRNA.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal modification in mammalian mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: m6A was initially discovered five decades ago.
source: Initially discovered five decades ago (Desrosiers et al., 1974; Perry and Kelley, 1974), research into this modification was catalyzed with the advent of transcriptome-wide detection methodologies, namely m6A-seq/m6A-meRIP (Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Desrosiers et al., 1974 and Perry and Kelley, 1974.

claim: Research into m6A was catalyzed with the advent of transcriptome-wide detection methodologies, namely m6A-seq/m6A-meRIP.
source: Initially discovered five decades ago (Desrosiers et al., 1974; Perry and Kelley, 1974), research into this modification was catalyzed with the advent of transcriptome-wide detection methodologies, namely m6A-seq/m6A-meRIP (Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dominissini et al., 2012 and Meyer et al., 2012.

claim: m6A-seq/m6A-meRIP methods rely on the immunoprecipitation of m6A-containing RNA fragments, followed by high-throughput sequencing.
source: These methods rely on the immunoprecipitation of m6A-containing RNA fragments, followed by high-throughput sequencing and facilitate the extent of m6A methylation stochiometry on the m6A-site, -gene (m6A-GI) and sample level (m6A-SI) (Dierks et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the methodology of m6A-seq/m6A-meRIP and is supported by citation to Dierks et al., 2021.

claim: The most consistently observed molecular outcome of m6A is cytoplasmic mRNA degradation.
source: Nonetheless, the most consistently observed molecular outcome of m6A is cytoplasmic mRNA degradation (Du et al., 2016; Lasman et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Li et al., 2018; Uzonyi et al., 2023; Zaccara and Jaffrey, 2020), mediated via cytoplasmic 'm6A readers' of the YTH family (Du et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating m6A-mediated degradation.

claim: m6A-mediated cytoplasmic mRNA degradation is mediated via cytoplasmic 'm6A readers' of the YTH family.
source: Nonetheless, the most consistently observed molecular outcome of m6A is cytoplasmic mRNA degradation (Du et al., 2016; Lasman et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Li et al., 2018; Uzonyi et al., 2023; Zaccara and Jaffrey, 2020), mediated via cytoplasmic 'm6A readers' of the YTH family (Du et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Du et al., 2016 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: In mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), m6A appears to be the predominant driver of mRNA stability, explaining roughly 30% of the variation in mRNA half-lives.
source: In mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), m6A appears to be the predominant driver of mRNA stability, explaining roughly 30% of the variation in mRNA half-lives (Dierks et al., 2021; Uzonyi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dierks et al., 2021 and Uzonyi et al., 2023.

claim: m6A profiles were found to be qualitatively similar across highly different cell types, developmental stages, and tissues.
source: Specifically, m6A profiles were found to be qualitatively similar across highly different cell types, developmental stages, and tissues (Liu et al., 2020; Schwartz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020 and Schwartz et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in m6A levels at a minority of sites have been reported across diverse systems, ranging from cellular responses to diverse stressors, infection, disease, and during development.
source: Nonetheless, changes in m6A levels – often at only a minority of sites – have been reported across diverse systems, ranging from cellular responses to diverse stressors, infection, disease, and during development (Anders et al., 2018; Knuckles et al., 2017; Lichinchi et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023; Su et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies reporting m6A changes.

claim: Studies have consistently found m6A levels across chromatin-associated, nucleoplasmic and cytoplasmic mRNA fractions to be very similar.
source: Similarly, in considering m6A levels across different compartments within cells, studies have consistently found m6A levels across chromatin-associated, nucleoplasmic and cytoplasmic mRNA fractions to be very similar (Ke et al., 2017; Roundtree et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ke et al., 2017 and Roundtree et al., 2017.

claim: Slightly higher m6A levels were observed within the chromatin-associated fraction in comparison to the nucleoplasmic and cytoplasmic fractions in one study.
source: Nonetheless, slightly higher levels within the chromatin-associated fraction in comparison to the nucleoplasmic and cytoplasmic fractions (Ke et al., 2017) were observed in one study, contrasting with a more recent study finding reduced m6A levels in chromatin-associated RNA (Tang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ke et al., 2017.

claim: A more recent study found reduced m6A levels in chromatin-associated RNA.
source: Nonetheless, slightly higher levels within the chromatin-associated fraction in comparison to the nucleoplasmic and cytoplasmic fractions (Ke et al., 2017) were observed in one study, contrasting with a more recent study finding reduced m6A levels in chromatin-associated RNA (Tang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2024 and Yang et al., 2022.

claim: m6A deposition is catalyzed via a megadalton 'm6A–writer' complex, in which METTL3 acts as the catalytic component.
source: m6A deposition is catalyzed via a megadalton 'm6A–writer' complex, in which METTL3 acts as the catalytic component.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the m6A methylation machinery.

claim: m6A is to a considerable extent hard-coded, governed by the presence of the m6A consensus motif (DRACH motif) and distance from splice sites.
source: m6A is to a considerable extent hard-coded, governed by the presence of the m6A consensus motif (DRACH motif) and distance from splice sites (Garcia-Campos et al., 2019; He et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2023; Uzonyi et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies on m6A deposition rules.

claim: The vast majority of the literature has focused on 'active' dynamics, wherein changes in m6A levels were proposed to be a consequence of changes in deposition or removal of m6A at specific sites.
source: The vast majority of the literature has focused on 'active' dynamics, wherein changes in m6A levels were proposed to be a consequence of changes in deposition or removal of m6A at specific sites (Hess et al., 2013; Knuckles et al., 2017; Su et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies proposing active regulation of m6A.

claim: 5mC DNA methylation during early development is primarily thought to be regulated passively via cell division, whereby each division results in a twofold dilution of the DNA 5mC content.
source: For example, 5mC DNA methylation during early development is primarily thought to be regulated passively via cell division, whereby each division results in a twofold dilution of the DNA 5mC content (Mayer et al., 2000; Rougier et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mayer et al., 2000 and Rougier et al., 1998.

claim: m6ADyn predicts that nuclear m6A levels per gene would be invariably higher than the corresponding cytoplasmic levels, given the selective removal of m6A-harboring transcripts from the cytoplasm.
source: A first prediction of m6ADyn concerns heterogeneity in m6A levels across subcellular fractions: m6ADyn predicts that nuclear m6A levels per gene would be invariably higher than the corresponding cytoplasmic levels, given the selective removal of m6A-harboring transcripts from the cytoplasm (γm6A = S * γA, with S > 1).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the m6ADyn model based on its assumptions.

claim: m6A levels were higher in the nuclear fraction both at the sample and at the gene level in NIH3T3 cells, with the vast majority of genes (~82%) exhibiting higher methylation levels in the nucleus.
source: Consistent with m6ADyn predictions, we found that m6A levels were higher in the nuclear fraction both at the sample and at the gene level, with the vast majority of genes (~82%) exhibiting higher methylation levels in the nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on experimental m6A-seq2 data from NIH3T3 cells shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The trend of higher nuclear m6A levels was recapitulated in an independent experiment performed in primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs).
source: These trends were also recapitulated in an independent experiment performed in primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from MEFs shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: m6ADyn predicts that m6A levels across the entire cell are higher in genes that are relatively more abundant in the nucleus.
source: A second prediction of m6ADyn concerns heterogeneity in m6A levels between genes: m6ADyn predicts that m6A levels across the entire cell are higher in genes that are relatively more abundant in the nucleus, given that they are least susceptible to m6A-dependent decay (Figure 2b, left).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the m6ADyn model shown in Figure 2b, left.

claim: m6A levels were higher in more nuclear localized genes in mESCs.
source: Correlating the WT fractionation data against a previously acquired dataset capturing m6A levels per gene in mESCs (Dierks et al., 2021) revealed that indeed m6A levels were higher in more nuclear localized genes, consistent with m6ADyn predictions (Figure 2b, right).
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation and m6A-seq data from mESCs shown in Figure 2b, right.

claim: Similar observations of higher m6A levels in more nuclear localized genes were made in NIH3T3 and in HEK293T cells.
source: We made similar observations also in NIH3T3 and in HEK293T cells for which we acquired fractionation data, confirming the robustness of these results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, f).
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data from NIH3T3 and HEK293T cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, f.

claim: GLORI-GIs showed a high correlation of R = 0.71 with m6A-seq-derived m6A-GIs.
source: A comparison of GLORI-GIs with our m6A-seq-derived m6A-GIs showed a high correlation of R = 0.71 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d), supporting the robustness of m6A-GIs.
evidence: This is based on comparison of GLORI and m6A-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: GLORI-GIs were higher in more nuclear genes.
source: Moreover, GLORI-GIs were higher in more nuclear genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), consistent with our observations on the basis of m6A-GIs.
evidence: This is based on GLORI data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: m6ADyn predicts that loss of methylation in genes that are highly methylated in wild-type conditions would lead to increased cytoplasmic presence, whereas such an effect would be less pronounced in poorly methylated genes.
source: m6ADyn predicts that loss of methylation (as in Mettl3 KO conditions) in genes that are highly methylated in wild-type conditions would lead to increased cytoplasmic presence (and hence reduced nuclear:cytoplasmic levels), whereas such an effect would be less pronounced in poorly methylated genes.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the m6ADyn model.

claim: Loss of m6A results in an increased propensity for highly methylated genes to become cytoplasmic in mESCs.
source: Consistently with this model prediction, a comparison of localization in WT and m6A-depleted mESCs revealed that loss of m6A results in an increased propensity for highly methylated genes to become cytoplasmic (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data comparing WT and Mettl3 KO mESCs shown in Figure 2c.

claim: m6ADyn predicts that cytoplasmic genes will be more susceptible to increased m6A-mediated decay.
source: m6ADyn predicts that (1) cytoplasmic genes will be more susceptible to increased m6A-mediated decay and (2) more methylated genes will undergo increased decay (Figure 2d, left).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the m6ADyn model shown in Figure 2d, left.

claim: m6ADyn predicts that more methylated genes will undergo increased decay.
source: m6ADyn predicts that (1) cytoplasmic genes will be more susceptible to increased m6A-mediated decay and (2) more methylated genes will undergo increased decay (Figure 2d, left).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the m6ADyn model shown in Figure 2d, left.

claim: The experimental data supported the dual impact of m6A levels and localization on mRNA stability.
source: Strikingly, the experimental data supported the dual, impact of m6A levels and localization on mRNA stability (Figure 2d, right).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from mESCs shown in Figure 2d, right.

claim: Among cytoplasmic genes, 44% of the variability in METTL3-dependent decay is attributable to m6A levels.
source: Here, however, analyzing this relationship through the lens of subcellular localization revealed that among cytoplasmic genes – most susceptible to m6A-dependent decay – the association between localization and m6A is substantially stronger, with 44% of the variability in METTL3-dependent decay being attributable to m6A levels.
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data from mESCs.

claim: Among nuclear genes, the association between m6A and METTL3-dependent decay is substantially weaker (R2 = 0.19).
source: Conversely, among nuclear genes this relationship is substantially weaker (R2 = 0.19).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data from mESCs.

claim: m6ADyn predicts that decreasing production values results in a decrease in m6A levels.
source: m6ADyn predicts that decreasing production values (i.e. decreasing ⍺ rates) results in a decrease in m6A levels.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the m6ADyn model.

claim: m6ADyn predicts that the rate at which m6A levels decrease is inversely correlated with mRNA stability.
source: Moreover, m6ADyn predicts that the rate at which m6A levels decrease is inversely correlated with mRNA stability, that is that m6A levels will decrease faster in more short-lived genes (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the m6ADyn model shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Gene-level measurements of m6A displayed a subtle yet consistent decrease in m6A levels following ActD treatment in mESC cells.
source: Consistent with the m6ADyn predictions (Figure 3b, left), gene-level measurements of m6A displayed a subtle yet consistent decrease in m6A levels (Figure 3b, right).
evidence: This is based on experimental m6A-seq2 data following ActD treatment shown in Figure 3b, right.

claim: Treatment of MCF7 cells with Camptothecin (CPT) led to reduced m6A levels, with much more dramatic effect sizes on both the sample and gene levels.
source: Similarly, treatment of MCF7 cells with Camptothecin (CPT), a topoisomerase inhibitor that stalls RNAPII elongation, thereby reducing production rates (Listerman et al., 2006), led to reduced m6A levels, in this case with much more dramatic effect sizes on both the sample and gene levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Figure 3c).
evidence: This is based on experimental m6A-seq2 data following CPT treatment shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The decrease in m6A following CPT treatment was stronger in genes with lower half-lives.
source: As predicted by m6ADyn (Figure 3d, left), the decrease in m6A was stronger in genes with lower half-lives (Figure 3d, right).
evidence: This is based on experimental m6A-seq2 data following CPT treatment shown in Figure 3d, right.

claim: m6ADyn predicts that elimination of m6A-dependent decay will result in increased overall methylation levels.
source: m6A-Dyn predicts that elimination of m6A-dependent decay (e.g. γm6A = γA) will result (1) in increased overall methylation levels (Figure 3e) and (2) in decreased nuclear/cytoplasm localization due to stabilization of cytoplasmic transcripts.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the m6ADyn model shown in Figure 3e.

claim: m6ADyn predicts that elimination of m6A-dependent decay will result in decreased nuclear/cytoplasm localization due to stabilization of cytoplasmic transcripts.
source: m6A-Dyn predicts that elimination of m6A-dependent decay (e.g. γm6A = γA) will result (1) in increased overall methylation levels (Figure 3e) and (2) in decreased nuclear/cytoplasm localization due to stabilization of cytoplasmic transcripts.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the m6ADyn model shown in Figure 3e.

claim: m6A-mediated decay is primarily thought to be mediated via the three cytoplasmic YTHDF proteins (YTHDF1, YTHDF2, YTHDF3).
source: Given that m6A-mediated decay is primarily thought to be mediated via the three cytoplasmic YTHDF proteins (YTHDF1, YTHDF2, YTHDF3) (Du et al., 2016; Lasman et al., 2020; Zaccara and Jaffrey, 2020), we next conducted a triple knockdown of the YTHDF proteins in NIH3T3 cells followed by whole-cell m6A-seq2 measurements and subcellular fractionation coupled with RNA-sequencing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Du et al., 2016, Lasman et al., 2020, and Zaccara and Jaffrey, 2020.

claim: Triple knockdown of YTHDF proteins substantially reduced RNA levels of YTHDF1 and YTHDF2, but did not reduce YTHDF3 levels.
source: While the knockdown substantially reduced RNA levels of YTHDF1 and YTHDF2, it did not reduce YTHDF3 levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is based on experimental RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: There was an overall increase, albeit subtle, in m6A levels on the gene and sample levels following triple knockdown of YTHDF proteins.
source: Nonetheless, there was an overall increase, albeit subtle, in m6A levels on the gene and sample levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e, Figure 3f).
evidence: This is based on experimental m6A-seq2 data following YTHDF knockdown shown in Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Following triple knockdown of YTHDF proteins, there was a reduction in the nuclear/cytoplasmic levels of more highly methylated genes.
source: Moreover, as anticipated by m6ADyn, we noted a reduction in the nuclear/cytoplasmic levels of more highly methylated genes following this perturbation (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data following YTHDF knockdown shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The cellular response to heat shock is well documented to be associated with significant alterations in mRNA metabolism, characterized by a pronounced decrease in global export and an increase in the production of heat stress response (HSR) genes.
source: The cellular response to heat shock is well documented to be associated with significant alterations in mRNA metabolism, characterized by a pronounced decrease in global export and an increase in the production of heat stress response (HSR) genes (Mahat et al., 2016; Shalgi et al., 2014; Trinklein et al., 2004a; Trinklein et al., 2004b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mahat et al., 2016, Shalgi et al., 2014, Trinklein et al., 2004a, and Trinklein et al., 2004b.

claim: The cellular heat shock response has been implicated in differential m6A methylation of heat shock response genes (HSR-gene) at hundreds of m6A sites.
source: Additionally, the cellular heat shock response has been implicated in differential m6A methylation of heat shock response genes (HSR-gene) at hundreds of m6A sites (Knuckles et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022; Meyer et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on m6A changes during heat shock.

claim: A dramatic increase in the nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio of mRNA was observed upon heat stress treatment in MEFs.
source: We observed a dramatic increase in the nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio of mRNA upon heat stress treatment (Figure 4b, c), consistent with previously documented nuclear retention of mRNA upon heat stress (Shalgi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on experimental FISH data shown in Figure 4b, c.

claim: The first principle component (PC1) of m6A-GIs captured a continuous increase (or decrease) of m6A methylation along the heat stress time course.
source: The first principle component (PC1) captured a continuous increase (or decrease) of m6A methylation along the heat stress time course (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis of m6A-seq2 data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Genes undergoing increased methylation upon heat stress (high PC1 genes) became dramatically more nuclear during heat stress.
source: Remarkably, we observed that the genes undergoing increased methylation upon heat stress (high PC1 genes) became dramatically more nuclear during heat stress (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data during heat stress shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Genes with decreased methylation (low PC1 genes) exhibited a reversed trend in nuclear localization during heat stress.
source: Conversely, the genes with decreased methylation (low PC1 genes) exhibited a reversed trend (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data during heat stress shown in Figure 4f.

claim: PC1 loading of genes and nuclear:cytoplasmic fractionation display a correlation of R = 0.4.
source: Overall, PC1 loading of genes and nuclear:cytoplasmic fractionation display a correlation of R = 0.4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Genes with high PC1 values in the WT experiment showed a similar trend of increased nuclear abundance upon heat stress also in the siWtap treated cells.
source: We found that genes with high PC1 values in the WT experiment showed a similar trend of increased nuclear abundance upon heat stress also in the siWtap treated cells, suggesting that m6A is unlikely to be the driver of these changes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data from siWtap treated cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: High PC1 genes (displaying induced m6A levels during heat stress) tend to have substantially higher turn-over rates (shorter half-lives) in comparison to low PC1 genes.
source: In our analysis of the dataset and attempting to understand why only certain genes exhibit induced m6A levels than others, we made two observations: First, high PC1 genes (displaying induced m6A levels during heat stress) tend to have substantially higher turn-over rates (shorter half-lives) in comparison to low PC1 genes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data comparing PC1 genes with half-life data.

claim: High PC1 genes become more nuclear upon heat stress.
source: Second, we observed that high PC1 genes become more nuclear upon heat stress (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: High PC1 genes were enriched in 'cellular stress response' gene ontology, comprising classical heat stress response (HSR-) genes.
source: A closer inspection of high PC1 genes (in which m6A is induced during the cellular stress response) revealed that these were enriched in 'cellular stress response' gene ontology, comprising classical heat stress response (HSR-) genes such as Hspa1a, Hspb1, Hsp1d, Hsp1e, Hsph1, and Dnajb1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Genes that showed the highest transcriptional induction are genes that have a high PC1 loading.
source: An analysis of Pro-seq data, which evaluates RNA Pol II occupancy as a proxy for transcriptional rate in MEFs during heat stress, confirmed that genes that showed the highest transcriptional induction are genes that have a high PC1 loading, that is show increased m6A level upon heat stress (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is based on analysis of Pro-seq data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: While HSF1-target genes remained expressed at basal levels also within HSF1-KO cells, their m6A dynamics were completely lost.
source: In stark contrast, while HSF1-target genes remained expressed at basal levels also within HSF1-KO cells, their m6A dynamics were completely lost (Figure 4i, top).
evidence: This is based on experimental m6A-seq2 data from HSF1-KO cells shown in Figure 4i, top.

claim: HSF1-target genes were no longer enriched in the nucleus in HSF1-KO cells during heat stress, in stark contrast to the HSF-independent counterparts.
source: Consistently, fractionation experiments in HSF1-KO cells revealed that HSF1-target genes were no longer enriched in the nucleus, in stark contrast to the HSF-independent counterparts.
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data from HSF1-KO cells.

claim: HSF1-target genes do not experience an increase in nuclear enrichment during heat stress in HSF1-KO cells, unlike in the wild-type cells.
source: Furthermore, fractionation experiments of heat stress treated HSF1-KO cells followed by RNA-seq confirmed that the HSF1-target genes do not experience an increase in nuclear enrichment during heat stress, unlike in the wild-type cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data from HSF1-KO cells during heat stress.

claim: HSF1-independent genes demonstrate a similar increase in nuclear enrichment in both HSF1-KO and wild-type cells during heat stress.
source: Conversely, HSF1-independent genes demonstrate a similar increase in nuclear enrichment in both HSF1-KO and wild-type cells (Figure 4j).
evidence: This is based on experimental fractionation data from HSF1-KO and WT cells shown in Figure 4j.

claim: During the heat stress response, m6A accumulates within a large set of genes, primarily within targets that undergo increased nuclear localization.
source: To summarize, our results indicate that during the heat stress response, m6A accumulates within a large set of genes, primarily within targets that undergo increased nuclear localization.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the heat stress experiments.

claim: The increase in nuclear localization during heat stress is likely primarily due to a block in export, but in a subset of genes due to increased transcription.
source: This is likely primarily due to a block in export, but – in a subset of genes – due to increased transcription.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental findings from the heat stress experiments.

claim: Recently, it was uncovered that m6A deposition could, to a considerable extent, be attributed to simple exclusion (100-nt rule), wherein m6A is installed by default at all eligible consensus motifs, unless they are within ~100 nt of a splice junction.
source: Recently, it was uncovered that m6A deposition could, to a considerable extent, be attributed to simple exclusion (100-nt rule), wherein m6A is installed by default at all eligible consensus motifs, unless they are within ~100 nt of a splice junction (Uzonyi et al., 2023) in which case their deposition is inhibited by the exon–junction complex (He et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2023; Uzonyi et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on m6A deposition rules.

claim: m6A deposition within ~100 nt of a splice junction is inhibited by the exon–junction complex.
source: Recently, it was uncovered that m6A deposition could, to a considerable extent, be attributed to simple exclusion (100-nt rule), wherein m6A is installed by default at all eligible consensus motifs, unless they are within ~100 nt of a splice junction (Uzonyi et al., 2023) in which case their deposition is inhibited by the exon–junction complex (He et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2023; Uzonyi et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2023, Luo et al., 2023, Uzonyi et al., 2023, and Yang et al., 2022.

claim: DNA methylation in mammalian systems is controlled primarily passively, by dilution of DNA methylation over the course of cellular divisions.
source: Nonetheless, considering the dramatic dynamics to which DNA methylation is subject in the germline, these are mediated primarily passively, by dilution of DNA methylation over the course of cellular divisions (Rougier et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rougier et al., 1998.

claim: In neural cells, differences in relative mRNA localization within cell bodies versus neurites could, to a considerable extent, be attributed to the stability of the mRNA.
source: Our findings also connect with recent findings in neural cells, revealing that differences in relative mRNA localization within cell bodies versus neurites could, to a considerable extent, be attributed to the stability of the mRNA.
evidence: This is a reference to recent findings in neural cells.

claim: mRNA localization in neurons had been primarily thought to be governed actively, via specific RNA binding proteins involved in directing mRNAs to their target locations.
source: While mRNA localization in neurons had been primarily thought to be governed actively, via specific RNA binding proteins involved in directing mRNAs to their target locations, this study thus proposed a passive model, wherein the inherent stability of an RNA plays a role in determining its relative localization (Loedige et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Loedige et al., 2023.

claim: A study proposed a passive model for neuronal mRNA localization, wherein the inherent stability of an RNA plays a role in determining its relative localization.
source: While mRNA localization in neurons had been primarily thought to be governed actively, via specific RNA binding proteins involved in directing mRNAs to their target locations, this study thus proposed a passive model, wherein the inherent stability of an RNA plays a role in determining its relative localization (Loedige et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Loedige et al., 2023.

claim: Changes in m6A levels, both across subcellular compartments and across stimuli, are relatively rare, and typically also subtle.
source: To conclude, it is important to highlight that changes in m6A levels, both across subcellular compartments and across stimuli, are relatively rare, and typically also subtle.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the findings of the study.

claim: Many changes in m6A levels, when present, may be accounted for by changes in mRNA metabolism, rather than by active control over m6A at specific sites.
source: Our findings suggest that many of these changes, when present, may be accounted for by changes in mRNA metabolism, rather than by active control over m6A at specific sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.
